before.title: 4-Speed Automatic Transmission Wear / Failure (RE4F04A)
before.description: The 4th-gen Maxima's 4-speed automatic (shared with the I30) is the drivetrain's known weak point. Neglected fluid-and-filter service lets debris and metal shards accumulate, leading to slipping, harsh or delayed engagement, failure to move in Drive, and eventual first-gear or full transmission failure. Owners widely report this unit as failure-prone when maintenance is skipped, making fluid history critical when buying one of these cars.
before.solution: Service the transmission fluid and filter on schedule with the correct Nissan-spec ATF; address slipping early. Once metal contamination or gear failure occurs, a rebuild or replacement unit is required. Verify parts availability for a good used or rebuilt transmission.

before.title: Catalytic Converter Premature Failure (Bank 1)
before.description: The Maxima VQ35DE is known for premature catalytic converter failure, particularly the Bank 1 (front) converter. Failure typically occurs between 80,000-120,000 miles. The catalyst substrate deteriorates, often triggered by oil consumption issues inherent to the VQ35DE, rich running conditions, or age. The pre-cat (close-coupled converter near the exhaust manifold) fails more often than the underbody converter due to extreme heat exposure.
before.solution: Replace the failed catalytic converter. OEM replacements cost $800-1,500 per converter. CARB-compliant aftermarket converters are available for $300-600. Before replacing, check for oil consumption or other issues causing catalyst poisoning. If both banks show codes, a complete exhaust manifold/cat assembly may be more cost-effective.
symptoms: Sulfur or rotten egg smell from exhaust

communityRecommendations.text: Fix oil consumption first if you have it - new cats will just fail again if the engine is burning oil

communityRecommendations.content: Walker catalytic converter — EPA-compliant direct fit

before.title: Crank/Cam Position Sensor Failure (No-Start, Random Stalling)
before.description: The crank and cam position sensors are a well-documented weak point on the 4th-generation VQ30DE Maxima. Internal solder joints and the sensor's electronics degrade with heat and age, producing intermittent or lost signal. This is the same failure mode Nissan later formally recalled on the 2000-2002 cars (NHTSA 03V455000) for improper solder joints; 1995-1999 owners experience identical symptoms without recall coverage. (Note: unlike the earlier VG30 engines, the A32 VQ30DE is distributorless with coil packs; the crank position REF sensor sits near the oil filter, the POS sensor at the rear of the oil pan, and the cam sensor at the front timing cover.)
before.solution: Confirm with a scan tool (P0335 / P0340). Replace the failed crank/cam position sensor; many mechanics recommend replacing the crank and both cam sensors together since they share the same aging failure. Use Hitachi/OEM units, as cheap aftermarket sensors frequently fail again quickly.

before.title: CVT Belt Slip at High Mileage
before.description: The Maxima equipped with the Jatco CVT experiences progressive belt slip as mileage increases, typically becoming noticeable after 100,000-130,000 miles. The steel push belt loses grip on the pulleys, causing delayed acceleration response, RPM flare under load, and a rubber-band effect. Heavy acceleration and towing/heavy loads accelerate wear. Unlike the Altima/Rogue CVT issues that often manifest earlier, the Maxima CVT tends to last longer but still develops this wear pattern.
before.solution: Regular CVT fluid changes every 30,000 miles with Nissan NS-3 fluid can delay onset. Once significant slip occurs, the CVT typically needs replacement ($3,500-5,500 installed). Rebuilt CVTs are available for $2,500-3,500 installed. Nissan extended the CVT warranty on some model years. Aftermarket CVT coolers can help extend CVT life.

communityRecommendations.text: Install an external CVT cooler and change fluid every 30k miles - many owners report getting 200k+ miles this way

communityRecommendations.content: CVT fluid specifically formulated for continuous variable transmissions
Replacement CVT transmission filter to maintain fluid cleanliness

before.title: Dashboard Cracking and Bubbling
before.description: The 6th generation Maxima (A34) is notorious for dashboard cracking, warping, and bubbling. The dashboard material degrades from UV exposure and heat, developing cracks that spread across the surface and a sticky, melting texture. This issue affects the top surface of the dashboard visible through the windshield. The problem is worse in southern/hot climates but occurs nationwide. A class-action lawsuit resulted in some settlements.
before.solution: Dashboard cover or cap ($50-150) to cover cosmetic damage. Full dashboard replacement from Nissan ($1,200-2,000 parts + labor). Aftermarket dashboard replacements/overlays available ($200-400). Some owners have successfully used vinyl wrap to cover mild cracking ($100-200 professional installation).
symptoms: Pieces of dashboard material flaking off

before.title: Distributor Oil Leak / Cap & Rotor Contamination (Failed O-Ring, VG30 3rd Gen)
before.description: The distributor on the 3rd-generation VG30E/VG30DE Maxima seals to the head with an O-ring. That O-ring hardens and cracks with age, letting oil seep into the distributor and coat the cap and rotor with oily black powder, causing misfire and driveability problems. Excess crankcase pressure from a clogged PCV valve pushes oil into the distributor and accelerates the problem. (This applies to the distributor-equipped VG30 engines; the 1995-1999 VQ30DE is distributorless with individual coil packs and does not have this failure mode.)
before.solution: Replace the distributor O-ring/shaft seal and clean or replace the cap and rotor; replace the PCV valve at the same time to relieve crankcase pressure. If oil has migrated into the crank angle sensor optics, the full distributor assembly may need replacement.
symptoms: Oil leak at rear of engine

before.title: EGR Passage / EGR Temperature Sensor Tube Carbon Clogging (P0400)
before.description: Nearly every high-mileage 4th-gen Maxima eventually sets a P0400 (EGR flow insufficient) code. The root cause is almost never the EGR valve itself; instead the small EGR pipe and the port where the EGR temperature sensor sits pack with carbon, so exhaust gas can no longer flow past the sensor and the ECU reports low EGR flow. It commonly appears alongside a P0325 knock-sensor 'ghost' code. This is a classic emissions-inspection failure item on these cars.
before.solution: Remove the EGR tube/passage and the EGR temperature sensor, then clear the carbon with a pick and carburetor cleaner; clean the ports and passages rather than replacing the valve. Inspect/replace the EGR temp sensor if damaged. Full EGR valve replacement is only needed if the valve itself is stuck.

P0400 identifies insufficient EGR flow and does not by itself identify the obstructed component.

Clean or replace only the component proven faulty and verify flow afterward. before.title: Engine / Motor Mount Deterioration (Idle Vibration & Clunk)
before.description: The Maxima uses four engine/transmission mounts: front and rear on the center crossmember, a passenger-side engine mount, and a driver-side transmission mount. The rubber cracks and separates with age and heat; the front and rear crossmember mounts fail most often, transmitting the V6's vibration into the cabin and producing clunks on shifts and acceleration.
before.solution: Inspect all four mounts and replace the failed units (commonly the front and rear crossmember mounts). Replace in sets to prevent premature failure of new parts; OEM mounts are preferred over aftermarket rubber that transmits more vibration.

before.title: Ignition Coil Failure (VQ35DE)
before.description: The VQ35DE engine in the 6th and 7th generation Maxima is prone to ignition coil failure. Coils typically fail one at a time, causing misfires on the affected cylinder. The rear bank (cylinders 1-3) coils fail more frequently due to heat soak from the firewall proximity. Coil failure is especially common after 60,000-80,000 miles and is one of the most reported Maxima issues.
before.solution: Replace failed ignition coil(s). It is recommended to replace all 6 coils at the same time along with spark plugs to prevent repeat failures. OEM Nissan coils cost $40-60 each; quality aftermarket (Hitachi, Denso) $25-40 each. Total parts for all 6: $150-360. Labor: $150-300 (rear bank is harder to access). DIY-friendly on front bank.

communityRecommendations.text: Replace all 6 coils at once even if only one is bad - the others are likely not far behind

communityRecommendations.content: OE-quality ignition coils restore reliable spark and eliminate misfires

before.title: Repeated Fuel Injector Leaks / Electrical Failure (VG30 3rd Gen)
before.description: The 3rd-generation (1989-1994) Maxima's VG30-series injectors are prone to failing electronically rather than from dirt, and the lower injector seals can fail to seat, leaking fuel into the cylinders. before.title: Steering Column Clunk and Intermediate Shaft Wear
before.description: The 7th and 8th generation Maxima develops a clunking or popping noise from the steering column area, particularly noticeable when turning the wheel at low speeds or going over bumps. The issue is caused by wear in the steering column intermediate shaft u-joint and/or the electric power steering column itself. The clunk can feel like play in the steering and is especially noticeable in cold weather.
before.solution: Lubricate the intermediate shaft u-joint with white lithium grease as a temporary fix ($10 DIY). If the u-joint is worn, replace the intermediate shaft ($200-400 parts, $150-250 labor). In some cases the electric power steering column assembly needs replacement ($600-1,200 parts + labor). Nissan issued TSB NTB16-011 for some model years.

before.title: Power Steering Rack Seal Leak and Pump Failure
before.description: The 2004-2008 Nissan Maxima (6th generation, A34) develops power steering fluid leaks from the steering rack seals, high-pressure hoses, and pump seals. The rack and pinion seals deteriorate from heat cycling and age, causing fluid seepage that progressively worsens. As fluid level drops, the power steering pump whines, groans, and eventually fails from running dry. Leaking power steering fluid can contact hot exhaust components, creating a fire hazard. Loss of power assist makes the vehicle difficult to steer, especially at low speeds and during parking maneuvers.
